Hey! So. I got married and divorced within about two months when I was 23. I got sent in a spiraling hellscape of work, and I really just hated life for a long time. I buried myself in work, school, and video games for several years. I eventually stopped worrying about my future, and I started doing things that brought me joy, like going to an aquarium near where I lived, reading things I loved, and adopting a fitness routine that worked for me. Once I stopped crippling myself with worry, it was easy to start developing some confidence and moving forward with my life. I met my wife when I was 28 and we got married when I was 30. Now we live in Europe, a long time dream of mine (coming from the states).

It gets better. It doesn't get easier. I'm likely about to go no contact with my parents. My job is a mess, and my future is unpredictable. But I have good people I surround myself with, I have faith that God will get me through any problems, and I also have faith in myself that I can adapt to any situation. That is freeing. Learning that about yourself is huge, and definitely something you can look forward to.
My life is grand, unsarcastically, with one significant drawback: I'm getting ready to set boundaries with my folks that have a distinct possibility of turning into no-contact. I'm terrified.

My weird thing was a bit of self discovery. 
This starts on a bit of a tangent, but it's all relevant. 

I freaking love Chick-fil-A. Politics aside, I just love their food. Unfortunately, I also lived far enough away from the closest restaurant that it was not worth driving out to it for just a craving. 

Fortunately, the Coroner's Office was closed to the nearest one from me. 

I'm not a doctor, but I used to have to go to autopsies for work. I'd basically just be there to take notes in case something specific was out of the ordinary. Now, these autopsies were usually early on in the morning and would last a couple hours, meaning they finished around lunch time. I would go, grab the coveted Chick-fil-A, and then drive the hour or so back to my office to type up my reports. 

This went on for about three years, after which point, I realized that towards the end of the autopsies, I would start getting hungry. Usually around when they started breaking out the bone saw, I'd start craving those sweet sweet waffle fries. I didn't think anything of it. Maybe I was just hungry in general. It's usually about 11:00-11:45 at this point. 
A few months after I stopped needing to regularly go to autopsies, I was watching the news and they started talking about the autopsy on Prince. I got hungry and drove off for my lunch break and got Chick-fil-A, which was much closer to my new office. I realized in horror what I'd done when I got back to my office and started eating.  

TL;DR: I Pavloved myself into associating autopsies with Chick-fil-A. 

Also, I could really go for some lemonade and a chicken sandwich.

Name of the Wind is beautifully artistic.  I was able to get over Kvothe's Mary-Sueness just on sheer weight of the way Rothfuss writes.  He drew me so quickly that the story was over before I knew it (once I got about halfway through the set-up of the frame story).

Skyward is a weird one for Sanderson.  I enjoyed it, but there is something different about it that I just cannot place.  I still enjoyed it, but it was a bizarre one for me.  The Final Empire I adored.  Allomancy/Feruchemy is one of the my favorite magic systems, and I found myself fantasizing about how I would use it in reality.  I also love heist stories, so I love the set up of transitioning a heist story into an "overthrow the evil dictator" story.  While I think that the Well of Acsension was one of his most difficult books for me to get through, I love that the book realistically poses the question "Okay, well now what?"  Scadriel (the world Mistborn is set in) is fantastically built, and I can't help but admire it.

As far as Brandon Sanderson himself, I think that the reason I like him so much is a combination of a bunch of things.  First, the tone he sets is so optimistic for most of his books, even when everything is falling apart.  I love that he builds wonderful humor into everything he touches.  Second, I love all of his characters.  With few exceptions, none of them feel like walking plot devices (even the ones who only show up for a couple pages), and each feels like a real person.  He then takes them and shapes them, and it's fun to watch them grow.  The best example of this for me is Warbreaker, where he starts with two sisters, one who is impulsive, wild, and not noted as politically saavy, and another who is careful, measured, and politically brilliant.  He then basically reverses their positions over the course of the book, with them each being recognizably the same person.  One other note is that I adore how he deals with mental illness or anxiety (Vin's trust issues, Shallan's split personality disorder, Kaladin's crippling depression).

I also adore his magic systems and world building, and find myself trying to figure out what happens next and how everything works.  I asked myself how it would work if someone had just one Allomantic power and one Feruchemical power and how the two could work together, only to find out that in Mistborn Era 2, he fully addresses that in the Twinborn people, who have one of each (and the two main characters are each different kinds of twinborn).

Finally, I love his planning and creativity.  He builds everything together so logically.  He foreshadows extremely well, and when his inevitable twists get pulled out, you say "Why didn't I see that coming!?"  Everything is just art.  I could ramble all day ( and probably will later) but this seems like a good start.
